question: A 28-year-old primigravida at 28 weeks has a haemoglobin of 10.2 g/dL with an MCV of 84 fL and no symptoms of anaemia. Which explanation best accounts for this finding?

answers.text: Iron-deficiency anaemia due to inadequate dietary intake during pregnancy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Although iron deficiency is common in pregnancy, a haemoglobin of 10.2 g/dL with a normal MCV (84 fL) at 28 weeks is more consistent with physiological haemodilution than iron deficiency (which causes microcytosis, MCV <80 fL).

answers.text: Physiological haemodilution, as plasma volume expansion (40–50%) exceeds red cell mass increase (~25%)

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! In pregnancy, plasma volume rises by 40–50% while red cell mass increases by only 20–30%. This disproportionate expansion causes a fall in haemoglobin concentration — the physiological anaemia of pregnancy. A haemoglobin ≥10.0 g/dL with normal indices at 28 weeks is expected.
Folate deficiency causes macrocytic anaemia (elevated MCV >100 fL). The normal MCV here makes this unlikely.

answers.text: Sickle cell disease decompensation triggered by the physiological demands of pregnancy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Sickle cell disease would be a known diagnosis with a characteristic blood film. A normocytic haemoglobin at 10.2 g/dL in a previously well woman at 28 weeks is most consistent with physiological haemodilution.

overallFeedback.feedback: Physiological haemodilution: plasma volume rises 40–50%, red cell mass only 20–30%. The net effect is a dilutional drop in haemoglobin — normal at 28 weeks if Hb ≥10 g/dL with normal MCV.

Correct! Physiological anaemia of pregnancy: plasma volume +45%, RBC mass +25% → haemoglobin dilution. WHO defines anaemia in pregnancy as Hb <11 g/dL (1st/3rd trimester) or <10.5 g/dL (2nd trimester).
